title: FAR U5·W3 — Fair Value, Nonmonetary Exchanges & Accounting Changes
lessonHtml:
Cold open — measurement and corrections

Three cross-cutting topics finish the measurement toolkit: how fair value is defined and ranked under ASC 820, how nonmonetary exchanges are recorded when one asset is swapped for another, and how accounting changes and errors are reported under ASC 250. Each appears across the statements — a Level 3 fair value, an equipment trade-in, a switch in inventory method — and each has a precise rule about what to record now and what to restate.

Fair value defined

Fair value (ASC 820) is an exit price — the price to sell an asset or transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. It is market-based, not entity-specific, and is measured in the principal market (or, absent one, the most advantageous market). Three valuation approaches may be used: the market approach (comparable prices), the income approach (discounted future cash flows), and the cost approach (current replacement cost). Fair value assumes the asset's highest and best use.

The fair-value hierarchy

ASC 820 ranks the inputs to a fair-value measurement, maximizing observable data. Level 1 inputs are quoted prices in active markets for identical assets (the most reliable). Level 2 inputs are observable but not Level 1 — quoted prices for similar assets, or observable rates and yields. Level 3 inputs are unobservable, reflecting the entity's own assumptions in a model (the least reliable, requiring the most disclosure). The level of the measurement is set by the lowest-level significant input, and the classification drives the audit scrutiny from AUD Unit 3.

Nonmonetary exchanges — the general rule

When a company swaps one nonmonetary asset for another (ASC 845), the general rule is to record the asset received at fair value and recognize the full gain or loss — the difference between the fair value and the book value of the asset given up. MBG trading a used loader plus cash for a different machine would normally recognize gain or loss immediately. The key question that can override this rule is whether the exchange has commercial substance.

Commercial substance and its exception

An exchange has commercial substance if the entity's future cash flows are expected to change significantly as a result (different amounts, timing, or risk). If it does, record at fair value and recognize the full gain or loss. If the exchange lacks commercial substance (e.g., trading similar assets), gains are generally deferred — the asset received is recorded at the book value (carryover basis) of the asset given up, so no gain is recognized (a loss is still recognized). The exception exists because a swap of essentially equivalent assets has not culminated an earnings process.

Boot in a no-commercial-substance exchange

A wrinkle arises when boot (cash) changes hands in an exchange lacking commercial substance. The party paying boot recognizes no gain. The party receiving boot recognizes a proportionate gain if the boot is less than 25% of the total consideration — the recognized gain equals total gain × (boot received ÷ total consideration received). If boot is 25% or more, the entire transaction is treated as monetary and both parties recognize the full gain. The 25% threshold is the dividing line tested on the exam.

Accounting changes — principle versus estimate

ASC 250 sorts changes into types with different treatments. A change in accounting principle (e.g., FIFO to weighted-average) is applied retrospectively — prior-period statements are restated and the cumulative effect adjusts the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented. A change in accounting estimate (revised useful life, bad-debt rate) is applied prospectively — only the current and future periods are affected, with no restatement. When a change in principle is inseparable from a change in estimate (such as a change in depreciation method), it is treated as a change in estimate — prospective.

Reporting-entity changes and error corrections

Two more categories complete the framework. A change in reporting entity (e.g., presenting consolidated rather than separate statements) is applied retrospectively for all periods presented. An error correction — a mistake in a previously issued statement (a math error, a misapplied principle, fraud) — is not an accounting change; it is corrected by restating the prior-period statements, with a prior-period adjustment to the beginning balance of retained earnings. Distinguishing an error (restate) from an estimate change (prospective) is a frequent exam trap, because both can involve a revised number.

Disclosures and the fair value of liabilities

ASC 820 also governs measuring a liability at fair value — the price to transfer it to a market participant, incorporating the entity's own nonperformance risk (including its credit standing). Extensive disclosures accompany fair-value measurement: the level of each measurement, the valuation techniques and inputs, and for recurring Level 3 items a reconciliation of beginning-to-ending balances and the sensitivity of the measurement to the unobservable inputs. The disclosure burden rises as the inputs become less observable, precisely because Level 3 estimates are the least verifiable.

Retrospective application and its limits

Applying a change in principle retrospectively means restating each prior period presented as if the new principle had always been used, then adjusting the opening balance of retained earnings for the cumulative effect on periods before the earliest one shown. When it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effects, the entity applies the new principle prospectively from the earliest date practicable. The goal of retrospective treatment is comparability — readers can compare years on a consistent basis — which is exactly why an error, which also distorts comparability, is likewise corrected by restatement rather than buried in current income.

Disclosing an accounting change

An accounting change carries its own disclosure requirements. For a change in principle, the entity discloses the nature and justification (why the new method is preferable), the method of applying it, and the effect on income, earnings per share, and the affected line items for each period presented. A material change in estimate is disclosed with its effect on current income. The disclosures let users understand why the comparatives moved — distinguishing a genuine economic change from a mere change in how the same events are reported.

CMA bridge

When MBG remeasures an asset to fair value, trades equipment, or switches an accounting method, FAR dictates the mechanics; the CMA program then explains the effect on the metrics. A retrospective principle change restates the comparatives the CFO presents to lenders, while an estimate change flows only forward — a distinction that matters when explaining a swing in reported results.

Practice and recap

  1. Define fair value as an exit price in the principal market; rank inputs Level 1 (quoted/identical) > Level 2 (observable) > Level 3 (unobservable), using the lowest significant input.
  2. Record nonmonetary exchanges at fair value with full gain/loss when there is commercial substance; defer gain (carryover basis) when there is none.
  3. Apply the boot rule for no-commercial-substance exchanges: payer recognizes no gain; receiver recognizes proportionate gain if boot < 25%, full gain if ≥ 25%.
  4. Classify ASC 250 changes: principle = retrospective; estimate = prospective; depreciation-method/inseparable = prospective (estimate); reporting entity = retrospective; error = restate (prior-period adjustment).

Recap: fair value is an exit price measured in the principal market, with inputs ranked Level 1 (quoted/identical) to Level 3 (unobservable) and the measurement set by the lowest significant input; nonmonetary exchanges record at fair value with full gain when they have commercial substance but defer gain at carryover basis when they do not (with a 25% boot threshold splitting proportionate from full gain recognition); and ASC 250 applies principle changes retrospectively, estimate changes (including depreciation-method changes) prospectively, reporting-entity changes retrospectively, and error corrections by restatement through a prior-period adjustment.

flashcards.back: Exit price to sell an asset / transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants, in the principal (or most advantageous) market. Market-based, not entity-specific.
Level 1: quoted prices, identical assets, active markets. Level 2: observable (similar assets, rates). Level 3: unobservable (model/own assumptions). Classified by the lowest significant input.
Record asset received at fair value; recognize full gain/loss (FV − book value of asset given up).
Future cash flows change significantly → fair value, full gain/loss. Lacks commercial substance → carryover (book) basis, defer gain (loss still recognized).
Payer of boot: no gain. Receiver: proportionate gain if boot < 25% [gain × boot/total]; full gain if boot ≥ 25% (treated as monetary, both recognize full gain).
Principle (e.g., FIFO→avg): retrospective, adjust opening retained earnings. Estimate (useful life, bad-debt %): prospective, no restatement.
A change in principle inseparable from a change in estimate → treated as a change in ESTIMATE → prospective.
Error in a prior issued statement → restate prior periods with a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings (not an accounting change). Estimate change → prospective.

questions.explain: Fair value is the exit price to sell/transfer in an orderly transaction in the principal market.

questions.q: A fair-value measurement using a quoted price for a similar (not identical) asset is:
questions.explain: Quoted prices for similar assets are observable Level 2 inputs; identical-asset quotes are Level 1.

questions.q: A nonmonetary exchange that LACKS commercial substance is generally recorded at:
choices: The carryover (book) basis of the asset given up, deferring gain
questions.explain: Without commercial substance, gains are deferred — the asset received is recorded at carryover basis.

questions.q: In an exchange lacking commercial substance, the party PAYING boot recognizes:
questions.explain: The payer of boot recognizes no gain; the receiver may recognize a proportionate gain if boot < 25%.

questions.q: A change from FIFO to weighted-average inventory is applied:
questions.explain: A change in accounting principle is applied retrospectively.

questions.q: A change in the estimated useful life of equipment is applied:
questions.explain: A change in estimate is prospective, affecting only current and future periods.

questions.q: Correcting an error in a previously issued financial statement requires:
choices: Restating prior periods with a prior-period adjustment to retained earnings
questions.explain: Errors are corrected by restating prior periods, with a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings.
